passages.happening:
“Now faith is the assurance of what we hope for and the certainty of what we do not see. This is why the ancients were commended” (verses 1-2).

“By faith we understand that the universe was formed at God’s command, so that what is seen was not made out of what was visible” (verse 3).
passages.hearers:
Chapter 10 ended with the words ‘My righteous one will live by faith’. Now the writer shows what that faith looks like, through the whole story of Israel's Scriptures.

‘Assurance’ translates a word that means what stands underneath, a foundation. It is the same word used in 1:3 for God's ‘nature’. Faith gives solid ground to things we hope for but cannot yet hold. ‘Certainty’ translates a word used for proof in an argument. Faith is sure of what it cannot see, because it trusts the God who promised.

This is not a full definition of everything faith is. It is a description of the kind of faith the readers needed: faith that looks ahead and keeps going when the promise has not yet come.

‘The ancients were commended’ means God gave his approval to the people of faith in the past. The rest of the chapter names them.

The list starts at the very beginning, with creation. We did not see the world being made. We believe God made it by his word, so that the things we see came from what cannot be seen.
passages.ot:
Verse 3 looks back to Genesis 1, where God speaks and things come to be: “And God said, ‘Let there be light,’ and there was light” (Genesis 1:3). The psalms say the same: “For He spoke, and it came to be; He commanded, and it stood firm” (Psalm 33:9).

Lists of heroes were a familiar way of teaching in Jewish writing. Hebrews' list is different in one way: its people are praised not for courage or wisdom, but for trusting God's promise.
passages.hard:
Does verse 3 settle questions about how and when the world was made?

No. It says that the world was made ‘at God’s command’, and that what we see came from what we cannot see. Christians confess together that God made all things. Verse 3 says that we know this ‘by faith’, by trusting God's word, not by having watched it happen.

It does not speak to the age of the earth or to how living things came to be. Christians who differ on those questions can read this verse together and say it with one voice. These notes do not take a side on them.
passages.asks: Faith is sure of what it cannot see. Ask what you are hoping for that you cannot yet see. Ask whether your hope stands on solid ground, on the God who spoke the world into being. And ask what it would look like to live today as if his promises are true.

passages.happening:
“By faith Abel offered God a better sacrifice than Cain did. By faith he was commended as righteous when God gave approval to his gifts. And by faith he still speaks, even though he is dead” (verse 4).

“By faith Enoch was taken up so that he did not see death: ‘He could not be found, because God had taken him away.’ For before he was taken, he was commended as one who pleased God” (verse 5).

“And without faith it is impossible to please God, because anyone who approaches Him must believe that He exists and that He rewards those who earnestly seek Him” (verse 6).

“By faith Noah, when warned about things not yet seen, in godly fear built an ark to save his family. By faith he condemned the world and became heir of the righteousness that comes by faith” (verse 7).
passages.hearers:
‘By faith’ is one word in Greek, and it begins sentence after sentence through the chapter, like a drumbeat.

Abel's sacrifice was ‘better’ than his brother Cain's. Genesis does not say exactly why. Hebrews says the difference was faith. Abel was killed by his brother, but ‘he still speaks’. His story still teaches.

Enoch ‘walked with God’, Genesis says, and then he was gone, because God took him. Hebrews reads that as a man who pleased God by trusting him.

Verse 6 is the heart of this passage. To come to God, you must believe two things: that he is there, and that he rewards those who seek him. Faith is not only believing that God exists. It is trusting that he is good to those who look for him.

Noah believed God's warning about a flood no one had seen. He built the ark, which must have looked foolish. His obedience showed up the unbelief of the world around him.
passages.ot:
Abel's story is in Genesis 4. Abel “brought the best portions of the firstborn of his flock. And the LORD looked with favor on Abel and his offering” (Genesis 4:4).

Enoch's is in Genesis 5: “Enoch walked with God, and then he was no more, because God had taken him away” (Genesis 5:24). Hebrews' wording, ‘He could not be found’, differs a little from the Hebrew, ‘he was no more’, since the writer usually follows the Greek Old Testament. The meaning is close.

Noah's is in Genesis 6 to 9: “So Noah did everything precisely as God had commanded him” (Genesis 6:22).
passages.asks: Without faith it is impossible to please God. Ask whether you believe not only that God exists, but that he rewards those who seek him. Ask where you are seeking him, and where you have stopped. And ask what God may be asking you to do that looks foolish to others, as the ark did.

passages.t: Abraham and Sarah: strangers looking for a city
passages.happening:
“By faith Abraham, when called to go to a place he would later receive as his inheritance, obeyed and went, without knowing where he was going” (verse 8). He lived in the promised land like a foreigner, in tents, with Isaac and Jacob. “For he was looking forward to the city with foundations, whose architect and builder is God” (verse 10).

“By faith Sarah, even though she was barren and beyond the proper age, was enabled to conceive a child, because she considered Him faithful who had promised” (verse 11). From Abraham, ‘as good as dead’, came descendants as many as the stars and the sand (verse 12).

“All these people died in faith, without having received the things they were promised. However, they saw them and welcomed them from afar. And they acknowledged that they were strangers and exiles on the earth” (verse 13). They were longing “for a better country, a heavenly one. Therefore God is not ashamed to be called their God, for He has prepared a city for them” (verse 16).
passages.hearers:
Abraham left his home without knowing where he was going. That is faith: trusting the one who calls more than the map.

He lived in the land God promised him, but he never owned it, apart from a field for a grave. He lived in tents, moving from place to place, like a foreigner. People who lived without citizenship in a place were called strangers or resident aliens, and they could be treated with suspicion. Hebrews says that is the normal life of faith. God's people do not fully belong to any city on earth. They are looking for the city God is building.

Sarah's faith is named too. She was past the age of having children, and she trusted the God who had promised. It is worth remembering that, at first, she laughed at the promise (Genesis 18:12). Hebrews does not hide that her faith grew.

Verses 13 to 16 are a pause. These people died before they saw the promise kept. They saw it ‘from afar’, like travellers seeing a city on the horizon. And ‘God is not ashamed to be called their God’. He calls himself ‘the God of Abraham, Isaac and Jacob’.
passages.ot:
God's call to Abraham is in Genesis 12: “Leave your country, your kindred, and your father’s household, and go to the land I will show you” (Genesis 12:1).

Abraham called himself what Hebrews calls him. When Sarah died he said to the people of the land, “I am a foreigner and an outsider among you. Give me a burial site among you so that I can bury my dead” (Genesis 23:4). That burial field was the only part of the land he ever owned.

Sarah laughed when she first heard the promise: “After I am worn out and my master is old, will I now have this pleasure?” (Genesis 18:12). Yet the son was born, and he was named Isaac, ‘he laughs’.

Israel's later singers knew they were strangers too: “For I am a foreigner dwelling with You, a stranger like all my fathers” (Psalm 39:12).
passages.hard:
Does being ‘strangers and exiles on the earth’ mean Christians should not care about the world, or about the places they live?

No. Abraham lived as a stranger in the land, and he still dug wells, made peace with his neighbours, bought a field honestly and buried his wife with honour. The prophet Jeremiah told Israel's exiles in Babylon, “Seek the prosperity of the city to which I have sent you as exiles” (Jeremiah 29:7).

Being strangers means not giving our final loyalty to any nation, city or party, because our true home is the city God is building. It frees believers to love their neighbours, whoever they are, without making any earthly place their god. It is never a reason to treat foreigners and strangers among us badly. Israel was told, “So you also must love the foreigner, since you yourselves were foreigners in the land of Egypt” (Deuteronomy 10:19).
passages.asks: Abraham went out not knowing where he was going. Ask where God may be calling you to trust him without a map. Ask whether you are at home in this world in a way that makes you forget the city to come. And ask how you treat the strangers around you, since God calls his people strangers too.

passages.t: Isaac offered, and blessings for the future
passages.happening:
“By faith Abraham, when he was tested, offered up Isaac on the altar. He who had received the promises was ready to offer his one and only son, even though God had said to him, ‘Through Isaac your offspring will be reckoned.’ Abraham reasoned that God could raise the dead, and in a sense, he did receive Isaac back from death” (verses 17-19).

“By faith Isaac blessed Jacob and Esau concerning the future. By faith Jacob, when he was dying, blessed each of Joseph’s sons and worshiped as he leaned on the top of his staff. By faith Joseph, when his end was near, spoke about the exodus of the Israelites and gave instructions about his bones” (verses 20-22).
passages.hearers:
The test of Abraham is the hardest story in Genesis. God had promised that Abraham's family would come through Isaac. Then God asked him to offer Isaac. Hebrews says Abraham reasoned that God could raise the dead, so the promise would still stand. In a sense, Isaac came back from death when God stopped Abraham's hand.

Then three dying men look to the future. Isaac blessed his sons. Jacob, near death, blessed Joseph's sons and worshipped. Joseph, at the end of his life in Egypt, told his family that God would bring them out, and asked them to carry his bones to the promised land. None of them saw it happen. All of them trusted that it would.
passages.ot:
The test of Abraham is in Genesis 22. Abraham told Isaac, “God Himself will provide the lamb for the burnt offering, my son” (Genesis 22:8). The promise about Isaac is from Genesis 21: “through Isaac your offspring will be reckoned” (Genesis 21:12).

Joseph's last words are in Genesis 50: “God will surely attend to you, and then you must carry my bones up from this place” (Genesis 50:25). Generations later, as Israel left Egypt, “Moses took the bones of Joseph with him” (Exodus 13:19).

Verse 21 has a small difference from Genesis. The Berean Standard Bible of Genesis 47:31 says that Israel “bowed in worship at the head of his bed”. Hebrews says he worshipped ‘as he leaned on the top of his staff’. In Hebrew, the words for ‘bed’ (mittah) and ‘staff’ (matteh) are written with the same three letters and differ only in their vowels. The Hebrew text as it was later marked with vowels reads ‘bed’. Hebrews, which usually follows the Greek Old Testament, reads ‘staff’. Both pictures show an old man worshipping God at the end of his life.
passages.hard:
God asked Abraham to offer his son. How can that be called faith, and what does it mean for us?

This is one of the hardest stories in the Bible, and the site's note on Genesis 22 sets out how Jewish and Christian readers have wrestled with it. Hebrews reads it this way: Abraham trusted that God would keep his promise about Isaac even if Isaac died, because God could raise the dead. And the story ends with God stopping Abraham and providing a ram in Isaac's place. Many readers, Jewish and Christian, think part of its point is that the God of Abraham is not like the gods who demanded children.

One thing must be said without any doubt. No one today is told by God to harm a child, or anyone else. This story has never been read in Jewish or Christian teaching as permission to hurt a child. If you hear a voice, or have a thought, telling you to harm a child or anyone else, do not act on it. Seek help at once: tell someone you trust, a doctor, or a pastor, today. If anyone is in immediate danger, call your local emergency number. The Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.
passages.asks: Isaac, Jacob and Joseph all looked ahead at the end of their lives. Ask what you hope to hand on to those who come after you. Ask what promise of God you are trusting that you may not see kept in your lifetime. And ask what it would mean to worship, as Jacob did, even at the end.

passages.happening:
“By faith Moses’ parents hid him for three months after his birth, because they saw that he was a beautiful child, and they were unafraid of the king’s edict” (verse 23).

“By faith Moses, when he was grown, refused to be called the son of Pharaoh’s daughter. He chose to suffer oppression with God’s people rather than to experience the fleeting enjoyment of sin. He valued disgrace for Christ above the treasures of Egypt, for he was looking ahead to his reward” (verses 24-26). By faith he left Egypt, kept the Passover, and led the people through the Red Sea (verses 27-29).

“By faith the walls of Jericho fell, after the people had marched around them for seven days. By faith the prostitute Rahab, because she welcomed the spies in peace, did not perish with those who were disobedient” (verses 30-31).
passages.hearers:
Moses' story begins with his parents' courage. Pharaoh had ordered Hebrew baby boys to be killed. They hid their son and were not afraid.

Moses grew up as a prince of Egypt. He could have kept its wealth and power. Instead, he chose to stand with his own people, slaves who were suffering. Hebrews says he ‘valued disgrace for Christ above the treasures of Egypt’. Moses did not know the name of Jesus. The writer means that Moses shared the kind of disgrace that God's anointed one would bear, choosing God's people and God's promise over comfort. It is the same disgrace the readers were bearing for Christ.

Moses' faith was not perfect. Exodus tells that he killed an Egyptian and fled (Exodus 2:11-15), and later he argued with God about being sent. Hebrews praises his trust, not every act.

Then the exodus: the Passover lamb's blood on the doorposts, and the crossing of the sea. And Jericho, whose walls fell after Israel simply marched and trusted.

Rahab was a Canaanite woman in Jericho, and a prostitute. Hebrews names her so, plainly. She hid Israel's spies because she believed that Israel's God was the true God. She was saved, and she lived among Israel from then on. Matthew lists her among the ancestors of Jesus (Matthew 1:5).
passages.ot:
Moses' birth is in Exodus 2: “When she saw that he was a beautiful child, she hid him for three months” (Exodus 2:2). The Passover is in Exodus 12, the crossing of the sea in Exodus 14, and the fall of Jericho in Joshua 6.

Rahab's words to the spies are in Joshua 2: “I know that the LORD has given you this land” and “for the LORD your God is God in the heavens above and on the earth below” (Joshua 2:9, 11). And Joshua 6 says, “Joshua spared Rahab the prostitute, with her father’s household and all who belonged to her” (Joshua 6:25).
passages.hard:
Why is Rahab, a prostitute who lied to protect the spies, held up as a hero of faith?

Hebrews does not praise everything Rahab did, any more than it praises Moses for killing a man. It praises her faith: at a moment that cost her everything, she trusted that Israel's God was the true God, and she acted on it. James praises her for the same reason (James 2:25).

Christians have long discussed her lie to the king's men. Some, following Augustine, hold that lying is always wrong, and that Rahab was praised for her kindness and faith in spite of the lie, as a new believer still learning God's ways. Others hold that deceiving those engaged in unjust violence is not the kind of lie the commandment forbids, and point to the Hebrew midwives who deceived Pharaoh (Exodus 1). These notes do not choose. Both sides agree that the story's focus is her faith and courage, and that it is not a general approval of deceit.

That a Canaanite woman with her past stands in this list is good news. God's people are not made of the respectable. They are made of people who trust him. Her life did not end in shame. She lived among God's people, and she became part of the family line of Jesus.
passages.asks: Moses chose disgrace with God's people over the treasures of Egypt. Ask what ‘treasures’ you might be holding on to instead of following Christ. Ask whether you look down on anyone because of their past, when God put Rahab in this list. And ask what step of trust God might be asking of you, even if it seems as strange as marching around a wall.

passages.t: Some were rescued, some were not
passages.happening:
“And what more shall I say? Time will not allow me to tell of Gideon, Barak, Samson, Jephthah, David, Samuel, and the prophets, who through faith conquered kingdoms, administered justice, and gained what was promised; who shut the mouths of lions, quenched the raging fire, and escaped the edge of the sword; who gained strength from weakness, became mighty in battle, and put foreign armies to flight. Women received back their dead, raised to life again” (verses 32-35).

“Others were tortured and refused their release, so that they might gain a better resurrection. Still others endured mocking and flogging, and even chains and imprisonment. They were stoned, they were sawed in two, they were put to death by the sword. They went around in sheepskins and goatskins, destitute, oppressed, and mistreated. The world was not worthy of them” (verses 35-38).

“These were all commended for their faith, yet they did not receive what was promised. God had planned something better for us, so that together with us they would be made perfect” (verses 39-40).
passages.hearers:
The writer speeds up. There are too many to tell.

Some names are from Judges and the books of Samuel. Others are hinted at. ‘Shut the mouths of lions’ recalls Daniel. ‘Quenched the raging fire’ recalls his three friends in the furnace. ‘Women received back their dead’ recalls two mothers whose sons were raised by Elijah and Elisha.

Then, halfway through verse 35, the story turns. ‘Others were tortured and refused their release.’ This most likely points to Jewish martyrs about 167 BC, under the Greek king Antiochus IV, who were tortured and would not deny God, trusting in the resurrection. ‘Sawed in two’ probably refers to an old Jewish tradition about the death of the prophet Isaiah. Hebrews draws on the whole memory of Israel.

Notice the turn. Some, by faith, escaped the sword. Others, by faith, died by it. Both had faith. Faith did not decide who was rescued.

‘The world was not worthy of them.’ The people the world threw out were worth more than the world.

And the last verses. None of them, not even the greatest, received the promise in full. God was waiting so that they would be made perfect ‘together with us’. The faithful of Israel and the believers in Jesus will reach the goal together. No one is finished without the others.
passages.ot:
The stories behind verses 32 to 35 fill the books of Judges, Samuel, Kings and Daniel. Daniel said, “My God sent His angel and shut the mouths of the lions” (Daniel 6:22). His friends told the king, “He is able to deliver us from the blazing fiery furnace” (Daniel 3:17), and then, “But even if He does not, let it be known to you, O king, that we will not serve your gods” (Daniel 3:18). Elijah gave a widow back her son (1 Kings 17), and Elisha the Shunammite woman hers (2 Kings 4).

The list of names is not in order: Barak lived before Gideon, and Jephthah before Samson. And the Old Testament does not hide their failures. Gideon asked for sign after sign. Samson was reckless and violent; his last act was a prayer for strength to take revenge (Judges 16:28). Jephthah made a rash vow that, on the most common reading, cost his daughter her life (Judges 11:30-31, 39); a smaller number of readers think she was given to lifelong service instead. The book of Judges tells these stories as signs of Israel's decline. Hebrews' list does not erase that verdict. It honours the moments when each one trusted God.
passages.hard:
If these people had faith, why were some of them tortured and killed? Does faith guarantee rescue?

No. This passage is one of the plainest answers in the Bible. Some, by faith, escaped the sword; others, by faith, were killed by it. Both are commended. Faith is trusting God, not a way of making him do what we want.

Some teachers say that if you have enough faith, God will always give you health, wealth and success. That teaching is an error. Hebrews 11 lists faithful people who were ‘destitute, oppressed, and mistreated’, and it says ‘the world was not worthy of them’. Their faith was not weak. Those who hold it are often sincere, but the teaching is wrong.

If you have prayed for someone to be rescued, from illness, from danger, from prison, from death, and the rescue did not come, this chapter does not say your prayer was too weak. The three friends in Daniel said God was able to deliver them, “But even if He does not” (Daniel 3:18), they would still trust him. Grief and confusion at such a loss are not a lack of faith. If the weight of it is heavy, please share it with someone you trust: a friend, a pastor, a counsellor. If the pain ever feels like more than you can bear, reach out today to a crisis line or emergency service. The Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.

Why include Jephthah or Samson at all? The writer does not praise all they did. God works through flawed people who trust him. That is good news, but it is not a blessing on every act of those named.
passages.asks: Some were rescued; some were not; all were faithful. Ask whether your faith depends on things going well. Ask what it would mean to say, with Daniel's friends, ‘even if He does not’. And ask what it means that the faithful of every age are waiting to be made perfect ‘together with us’.
